questions.heading: Delay Changes Every Measure, Not Only NPV
questions.stem: Project R may start in 2028 or in 2030, so the model has two start variables for it. How should the value function give R its objective coefficients?

options.text: Two coefficients, each one built from the benefits of starting in that year
options.says: Right: every measure depends on the start year, so each start gets its own coefficient.

options.text: One coefficient, built from its earliest start, shared by both of its variables
options.says: Then the model sees no cost in delay; the lesson gives each start its own value.

options.text: Two coefficients, the later one smaller in every measure than the earlier one
options.says: Not every measure falls with delay: P035's reliability part grows while its NPV falls faster.

options.text: One coefficient, built from the average of its two starts' benefits
options.says: An average blurs the two starts together; each start year needs its own coefficient.

questions.heading: Value Points Restate as NPV-Equivalent Dollars
questions.stem: A value function uses a financial weight of 0.2 and a financial reference of $5,000k. One start's coefficient is 0.3 value points. What is that start worth in NPV-equivalent dollars?

options.text: $300k, from multiplying the points by the reference and by the financial weight
options.says: One $k earns w / R points, so points convert to $k by R / w: divide by the weight.

options.text: $1,500k, from multiplying the points by the reference and leaving out the weight
options.says: The financial weight belongs in the conversion; without it the dollars are 0.2 times too few.

options.text: $7,500k, from multiplying the points by the reference over the financial weight
$0.06k, from multiplying the points by the financial weight and leaving out the reference
options.says: Points become dollars through the financial reference and weight together: R / w.

questions.heading: The Plan's Value Is a Linear Expression in the Start Variables
questions.stem: A planner asks that the objective count the plan's total reliability score only up to 1, the reference, and nothing above it. What does that request do to the model's objective?

options.text: Nothing to the objective, since the cap is worked out before the model is built
options.says: The plan's total depends on which starts are chosen, so it cannot be worked out beforehand.

options.text: It makes the objective nonlinear in the starts, so it needs extra variables and rows
options.says: Right: a rule about the plan as a whole is not one coefficient per start.

options.text: It makes the reliability coefficients negative past the cap, so the objective stays linear
options.says: A coefficient belongs to one start; it cannot know when the plan's total passes the cap.

options.text: It lowers the reliability weight only, since a cap does what a smaller weight does
options.says: A cap counts each unit in full below it and not at all above; a weight scales every unit alike.
